text:
Candidate-conditioned history aggregation has clear precedents. [FISM (2013)](https://experts.umn.edu/en/publications/fism-factored-item-similarity-models-for-top-n-recommender-system/) learns item–item similarities through factorized embeddings and aggregates historical-item contributions; its history weights are not candidate-conditioned attention. [NAIS](https://arxiv.org/html/1809.07053) directly adds attention over historical items conditioned on the target item, including smoothed normalization to handle varying history lengths. [DIN](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.06978) likewise uses a local activation network to produce different history representations for different candidate ads. Thus, candidate-conditioned aggregation alone provides little basis for an originality claim.

[SASRec](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.09781) uses causal self-attention to encode an ordered history, then scores candidates against the resulting representation; the history encoding itself is candidate-independent. Candidate-conditioned pooling over SASRec states therefore adds a distinct scoring mechanism, but closely follows NAIS/DIN’s established principle. Useful simpler baselines: FISM-style normalized sum; candidate–history cosine similarities aggregated by mean or maximum; mean of the top-k similarities; temperature-controlled softmax pooling; and a small NAIS/DIN-style attention network. These are proposed ablations, not evidence of benchmark superiority. Compare raw item embeddings versus contextual SASRec states, cosine versus dot product, and all-history versus top-k pooling under the same validation protocol. Top-k cosine pooling should be treated as a simple sparse similarity baseline; this search does not establish whether the exact combination is novel. Candidate-specific scoring also warrants measuring full-catalog inference cost.
